title: Which short daily exercises sharpen your thinking and voice for case interviews?
description: Ten short daily exercises for case interview prep: recaps, speed maths, articulation, pacing, pauses and staying calm.
hook: The short daily exercises that help most are a 60-second recap, structure recall and speed maths for your thinking; paced reading, pause practice and "explain to the CEO" for your voice; and a little business reading and slow breathing for language and calm. Below are ten in all, each with how long to spend and what it trains. Pick the two or three that target your weakest area and do them most days, rather than trying all ten.
body:
How to use this list

Choose by weakness, not by what is enjoyable. If you lose the thread mid-case, lean on the thinking exercises. If people say you rush or mumble, lean on the voice ones. Fifteen minutes most days does more than two hours on a Sunday. A sample day might be ten minutes of speed maths, three minutes of pause practice and two minutes of breathing.

Thinking exercises

1. 60-second recap thinking

Play two minutes of a business podcast, pause, and recap it aloud in 60 seconds, starting "Three things were said". Do three to five a session. This trains summing up under time pressure, which is the core skill behind chart insights and recommendations.

2. Structure recall thinking

Read one of the core frameworks, close it, redraw it from memory, then check the gaps. One or two a day. This trains recalling a structure when you are under stress, so you adapt it rather than freeze.

3. Speed maths thinking

Ten minutes of the case maths drill: percentages, big multiplications, break-evens. Accuracy first, then speed. Faster arithmetic leaves more attention for thinking about what the number means.

4. Dual n-back thinking

Any dual n-back app, for ten minutes. Start at 2-back and move up only when you are above 80% accuracy. It trains holding several things in mind at once, but evidence that it improves performance in tasks like interviews is limited, so treat it as optional and put the other three first.

Voice exercises

5. Articulation voice

Two or three tongue twisters, first slow and exaggerated, then at speed. Three minutes before a mock. This gives you crisp diction, so every number you say is heard the first time.

6. Paced reading voice

Read a business article aloud for five minutes, slightly slower than feels natural, stopping at every full stop. This trains control of your pace, which most people lose when nervous.

7. Pause practice voice

Record a two-minute answer, count your "ums", then re-record it with a silent pause wherever a filler was. One answer a day. This replaces filler words with pauses, which sound more confident.

8. Explain to the CEO voice

Explain any formula or framework aloud in 60 seconds to an imaginary busy executive: answer first, no jargon. One or two a day. This trains top-down delivery.

Business language and calm

9. Read and listen business language

Fifteen minutes of a strategy book, business press or a CEO interview. Note one company story and one useful phrase. Over a few weeks this gives you vocabulary and real examples to draw on in cases.

10. Breathe calm

A few minutes of slow, breath-focused practice daily, and two minutes of box breathing (in for four, hold for four, out for four, hold for four) before every mock and interview. Many people find it gives them a calmer baseline and a faster recovery when a case goes wrong. More on this in staying calm when nerves hit.

Pick a routine by weakness

If your problem is...Do theseTime
Losing the thread mid-caseRecap, structure recall10 min
Slow or error-prone mathsSpeed maths, explain to the CEO12 min
Rushing, fillers, mumblingPaced reading, pause practice, articulation13 min
NervesBreathe, pause practice8 min
Thin business vocabularyRead and listen, explain to the CEO17 min

Test whether it is working

Drills only matter if they improve your cases. After each week, run one unfamiliar case with a partner and check the errors that matter: an unclear objective, an overlapping structure, wrong units, weak prioritisation or an unsupported recommendation.

If you can answer more maths questions but still lose track when explaining calculations aloud, move some practice to spoken business problems. If you read charts faster but miss the implication, add a one-sentence "so what" after every drill. Keep a simple log with three columns: the mistake, its cause and your next practice action. The value is in targeted correction, not in a tracker full of activity counts.

Common mistakes

  • Doing all ten. You will stop within a week. Two or three, done consistently, is the goal.
  • Practising only strengths. The drill you avoid is usually the one you need.
  • Silent practice. The interview is spoken, so most of these should be too.
  • Treating a drill score as the goal. A higher n-back level is not an offer. Check transfer to real cases.

Try it now

1. Explain to the CEO: what is break-even, in under 60 seconds, with a gym as the example?

Show the answer

"Break-even is the number of customers at which profit is zero. Divide fixed costs by what each customer contributes after variable costs. If the gym has $300k of fixed costs a year and each member contributes $25 a month, that's $300 a year, so it needs $300k ÷ $300 = 1,000 members to break even."

2. Speed maths, out loud: what is 15% of $640k?

Show the answer

"10% is $64k, 5% is half that, $32k, so 15% is $96k."

3. You keep forgetting the client's goal after a long calculation. Which exercises would you pick?

Show the answer

The 60-second recap and structure recall, plus one habit in every mock: write the goal in a box at the top of your page and link each result back to it.

Where to practise next

For the thinking drills in more depth, read ten minutes a day of case thinking; for the voice drills, speaking more clearly. The interview skills page links to free tools for each routine.
